selection_reason: 1. Evidence: No experiments have been run yet, so I am relying on priors. In cellular profiling, combining modalities and aggregating across several profiles usually helps. Learned set aggregators such as a transformer can also capture more than average pooling. 2. Test: config_033 sets a high-capacity anchor that combines multimodal input, multiprofile input and transformer aggregation. It uses the compact scVI latent space for RNA and the strong ViT-L image encoder, joined by weighted fusion. 3. Why now: If this full configuration scores well, later experiments can vary one factor at a time, such as the RNA encoder, image encoder, fusion type or pooling, to exploit it efficiently. If it underperforms, that is an early signal to test simpler setups like avgpool, single-modality or single-profile. Either result is informative for the remaining 9 experiments.

1. Evidence: there is only one result so far. The multimodal, multiprofile setup with scVI RNA, ViT-L image, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion (config_033) reached 0.725 accuracy and 0.685 F1. There is nothing to compare it against yet, so the importance of each design choice is still unknown. 2. Test: config_004 keeps every setting the same except the RNA encoder, which changes from scvi_n200 to pca_n2000. This isolates whether the RNA representation, likely a high-impact choice, drives performance. 3. Why now: a one-factor change from the only known reference point gives a clean, interpretable comparison. It also has a fair chance of beating the current best, since high-dimensional PCA features can keep more signal than a 200-dimensional latent space. Together this gives both information and a shot at improvement early in the budget.

1. Evidence: The two runs differed only in RNA encoder (multimodal, multiprofile, imagenet_vit_l, transformer, weighted). scvi_n200 beat pca_n2000 by about 14 points in accuracy (0.725 vs 0.586), and F1 agreed. The RNA encoder looks like a high-impact choice, but scgpt, the third option, is untested. 2. Test: config_041 keeps every other setting fixed and swaps in scgpt. This completes a controlled comparison of all three RNA encoders on the current best backbone and shows whether scgpt can beat scvi_n200. 3. Why now: settling the most influential choice early, before tuning smaller settings like fusion (concat vs weighted) or aggregation (avgpool vs transformer), keeps the remaining 6 experiments focused on the best encoder.

1. Evidence: with image encoder (ViT-L), aggregation (transformer) and fusion (weighted) held fixed, the RNA encoder sweep favors scvi_n200 clearly. It scored 0.725 accuracy, versus 0.586 for pca_n2000 and 0.520 for scGPT, and F1 follows the same order. The gap is large enough to anchor further search on scVI. The aggregation, fusion and image-encoder choices remain untested. 2. Test: config_034 keeps the best setup and changes only aggregation, from transformer to avgpool. This shows whether the transformer aggregator adds to the multiprofile gain or whether simple pooling does as well or better. 3. Why now: this is a one-factor change around the current best, so any difference can be attributed to aggregation. That also makes it a strong candidate for improving the best score. Six experiments will remain to test fusion (config_027), image encoder (config_025) and RNA-only baselines afterward.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder. It reached 0.725 accuracy, against 0.586 for pca_n2000 and 0.520 for scgpt. Transformer aggregation was slightly better than avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706, with F1 agreeing). However, every run so far has used weighted fusion, so the fusion choice is completely untested. 2) This run keeps the best configuration (scvi_n200, imagenet_vit_l, multiprofile, transformer) and switches only the fusion from weighted to concat. Any change in accuracy can then be attributed to the fusion method. 3) Fusion is a major untested design axis, and this is the cheapest clean test of it near the current best. With 5 runs left, it either finds a better configuration directly or confirms weighted fusion. That leaves later runs for other open questions such as the image encoder (resnet50) and single- versus multi-profile.

1) Evidence: scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.725 vs 0.586 for PCA and 0.520 for scGPT). Transformer aggregation and weighted fusion are only slightly better than avgpool (0.706) and concat (0.721), so those choices are close to settled. The image encoder is a major design choice that has not been tested, because every run so far used imagenet_vit_l. 2) This run keeps the best configuration (scVI, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. That isolates whether the image backbone matters and whether it can beat 0.725. 3) It is the best use of the budget because it is a controlled one-variable change around the current best, on an untested axis that could shift accuracy substantially. Its result will also guide the remaining runs, for example single-profile or RNA-only checks.

Evidence: the RNA encoder is by far the largest driver so far. scVI reaches 0.71-0.72, PCA 0.59 and scGPT 0.52. In contrast, changing the image encoder (ViT-L vs ResNet50), aggregation (transformer vs avgpool) and fusion (weighted vs concat) moved accuracy by only about 0.004-0.019. The best result so far is config_033 (scVI + ViT-L, transformer, weighted) at 0.725. Uncertainty: every run so far has been multimodal, so we do not know whether the image branch actually helps or just adds noise to a strong scVI signal. Test: config_031 is RNA-only with scVI, multiprofile and transformer aggregation. Compared with config_033, it isolates what the image modality contributes. Why now: further small tweaks to the multimodal setup look like diminishing returns. This experiment checks an untested, high-impact design choice that could beat the current best. If it falls short, it confirms that multimodal fusion helps and points the remaining 3 runs toward refining multimodal combinations, such as scVI + ResNet50 with concat.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.70–0.725 vs ≤0.59 for pca_n2000 and scgpt), and transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706). Multimodal also beats rna_only (0.725 vs 0.653). Within the scVI + transformer setting, the image encoder and fusion choices give close results. ViT-L with weighted fusion leads at 0.725, concat follows at 0.721, and ResNet50 with weighted fusion scores 0.713 but has the highest F1 (0.695). 2) Test: config_036 (scVI, ResNet50, transformer, concat) is the only untested combination in this top region. It checks whether ResNet50's stronger F1 pairs with concat fusion to beat the current best. 3) Why now: with 2 experiments left after this one, the strongest-evidence region should be finished before anything else. The settings already shown to be weaker (other RNA encoders, avgpool, single-profile or unimodal models) are unlikely to exceed 0.725, so this is the most promising use of the budget.

Evidence: the best result so far is scvi_n200 + imagenet_vit_l + transformer + weighted (config_033, 0.725 acc). scvi_n200 clearly beats pca_n2000 and scgpt. Transformer beats avgpool, and weighted fusion slightly beats concat. All eight runs so far used multiprofile, so the profile setting is still completely untested. The remaining scvi multiprofile options (config_012, 016, 044) each combine avgpool with concat and/or resnet50, which have each scored lower before, so they are unlikely to beat 0.725. This experiment tests config_042, which keeps the best encoders and weighted fusion but switches to singleprofile. It shows whether multiprofile aggregation is actually needed or whether a simpler single-profile model can match or beat it. It is the best use of the second-to-last run because it is the only untested design dimension that could plausibly lift the best score. The final experiment can then exploit whichever profile setting wins.

1) Evidence: scVI-n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.70–0.725 versus ≤0.59 for PCA and scGPT), and multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile. The best result so far is config_033 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted, 0.725). Swapping weighted for concat with ViT-L cost little (0.721). Swapping transformer for avgpool also cost little (0.706). 2) Test: config_012 (scVI + ViT-L + avgpool + concat) is one of only three untested scVI multimodal multiprofile configurations. It checks whether combining concat fusion with avgpool aggregation, under ViT-L, holds up or matches the top results. 3) Rationale: this is the final run, so the priority is the highest expected accuracy rather than exploration. The other two options, config_016 and config_044, use ResNet50, where concat caused a larger drop (0.688 versus 0.713). This makes config_012 the most promising remaining candidate within the strong scVI/ViT-L family, though it is unlikely to clearly beat 0.725.

1) No experiments have been run yet, so there is no direct evidence. Priors from multimodal cell profiling suggest that combining RNA and imaging, aggregating over multiple profiles, and using strong pretrained encoders tend to help. 2) config_051 tests the most expressive point in the space: multimodal, multiprofile, scGPT RNA encoder, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation and weighted fusion. Its result gives a strong anchor for the likely upper region of performance. 3) With only 10 experiments and only the best accuracy counting, starting from a likely high performer is the best opening move. Later runs can then vary one factor at a time from this anchor (encoders, aggregation, fusion, unimodal ablations) to find out which choices actually matter and to exploit the most promising direction.

1) Evidence: we have one result. The multimodal, multiprofile config_051 (scGPT + ViT-L, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) reached 0.520 accuracy and 0.479 F1. A single point says nothing yet about which design choices matter. 2) Test: config_014 keeps the same encoders and fusion but switches to singleprofile, with no aggregation. That makes it a one-factor test of whether multiprofile aggregation helps. 3) Why now: the profile setting is a high-level structural choice that determines which part of the remaining space to search. Settling it early gives the most information for steering the 8 experiments left.

Evidence: the multiprofile setup (config_051, 0.520 accuracy) clearly beat singleprofile (config_014, 0.422) with the same scGPT + ViT-L + weighted fusion setup. This is a large gap on both accuracy and F1, so multiprofile is the promising direction to keep. Within multiprofile, aggregation is the design choice that comes with it, and we have no evidence yet on transformer versus avgpool. Test: config_049 keeps everything from the current best and changes only transformer to avgpool, so any difference can be attributed to aggregation. Why now: it exploits the strongest result while resolving a key uncertainty. Knowing which aggregation works best will guide the remaining experiments on fusion, RNA encoder and image encoder.

1) Evidence: Multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile, at about 0.52–0.54 versus 0.42 accuracy. Within multiprofile, avgpool (0.542 accuracy, 0.483 F1) is slightly ahead of transformer (0.520, 0.479), but that gap is small. The fusion choice has never been varied, since every run so far used weighted fusion. 2) Test: config_038 keeps the current best setup (multiprofile, scGPT, ViT-L, avgpool) and swaps only weighted fusion for concat. This isolates the effect of the fusion strategy on a strong baseline. 3) Why now: fusion is a core multimodal design choice that applies to all remaining multimodal candidates. A one-factor change from the best configuration either finds a better model directly or rules out concat cheaply. That narrows the search before we spend later experiments on the RNA encoder (scVI or PCA) and the image encoder (ResNet50).

1) Evidence: multiprofile clearly beats singleprofile (0.52-0.54 vs 0.42). Within multiprofile, avgpool with weighted fusion is best so far (config_049, 0.542 accuracy, 0.483 F1). It edges out transformer aggregation and concat fusion, but those gaps are small. Every run so far has used scGPT with ViT-L, so the choice of RNA encoder is completely untested and is the largest remaining uncertainty. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted) and swaps scGPT for PCA (pca_n2000). It tests whether a simple high-dimensional RNA representation, which often rivals foundation-model embeddings, improves on scGPT. 3) Changing only one factor relative to the current best gives a clean comparison on an important design axis. It also has a real chance of producing a new best. Remaining budget can then go to scVI or the image encoder, depending on the result.

1. Evidence: the RNA encoder is the strongest lever found so far. Swapping scGPT for pca_n2000 in the same multiprofile, ViT-L, avgpool, weighted setup raised accuracy from 0.542 to 0.635 and F1 from 0.483 to 0.618. That gap is much larger than the aggregation or fusion differences seen under scGPT (about 0.02). The third RNA encoder, scvi_n200, is still untested. 2. This experiment keeps every other part of the best setup fixed and swaps in scvi_n200. It tells us directly whether scVI beats PCA and completes the RNA encoder comparison. 3. With 4 experiments left, settling the most influential design choice first is the best use of budget. If scVI wins, later runs can refine it. If not, we confirm pca_n2000 and spend the rest on image encoder, aggregation, fusion, or an RNA-only check.

1) Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far. Swapping scGPT for scVI raised accuracy from 0.542 to 0.706, with F1 rising from 0.483 to 0.667. Among scGPT runs, avgpool with weighted fusion was slightly best, though transformer and concat were close and that is only one comparison. The image encoder has never been varied: every run used imagenet_vit_l. 2) This experiment keeps the best setup (multiprofile, scVI, avgpool, weighted fusion) and swaps only the image encoder to resnet50. That isolates the effect of the one design choice not yet tested. 3) With 3 experiments left after this one, resolving the image encoder now shows which backbone to carry into the final runs. Those runs can then refine aggregation or fusion, or check whether the image branch helps at all with an scVI RNA-only run. This is likely more valuable than small aggregation or fusion tweaks, which have shown only modest effects so far.

1. Evidence: the RNA encoder is the dominant factor so far (scvi_n200 > pca_n2000 > scgpt). The best run is config_041 (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + avgpool + weighted, 0.706 accuracy). Swapping in ResNet50 cost only about 0.03, so the image encoder matters less. Aggregation and fusion were only compared under the weak scgpt encoder, where both differences were small and inconclusive. Transformer was about 0.02 below avgpool, and concat was about 0.02 lower in accuracy with roughly equal F1. 2. Test: this run keeps the best setup (scvi_n200 + ViT-L + weighted) and switches aggregation to transformer. It shows whether the more expressive set aggregator helps once the RNA features are informative, which the scgpt comparison could not show. 3. Why now: it directly exploits the best region and resolves the main open design choice there. Fusion (config_046) or an RNA-only check (config_024) can follow with the 2 remaining experiments.

Evidence: the best result so far is config_028 (scVI + ViT-L + transformer + weighted fusion, 0.725 accuracy, 0.685 F1). Earlier runs consistently favor scVI over PCA and scGPT, ViT-L over ResNet50 (0.706 vs 0.678), and multiprofile over singleprofile. Transformer aggregation slightly beat avgpool when paired with scVI. The main open question near the top is fusion. The only concat-versus-weighted comparison used scGPT with avgpool, where weighted won on accuracy (0.542 vs 0.518) but F1 was nearly identical (0.483 vs 0.484). That is weak evidence, and it may not hold with a stronger RNA encoder. This experiment keeps every winning choice and swaps only weighted fusion for concat, so it directly tests whether fusion type matters for the best setup. It is the best use of the second-to-last experiment because it changes only the least-settled design choice next to the current best. The alternatives each change a better-supported choice: config_033 swaps in the weaker ResNet50 encoder, and config_047 drops the image modality entirely.

1. Evidence: the best result so far is scvi_n200 + ViT-L + transformer aggregation (0.725 accuracy with weighted fusion, 0.721 with concat). scVI is clearly the strongest RNA encoder, ahead of PCA and well ahead of scGPT. Transformer aggregation beats avgpool, and fusion type barely matters. ResNet50 scored below ViT-L in the matched avgpool comparison, so config_033 and config_035 will most likely fall short of the current best. Avgpool variants such as config_046 are also likely to fall short. 2. This experiment tests the remaining open question: how much the image branch actually adds on top of the scVI transformer. Every result so far is multimodal, so an RNA-only scVI transformer model has never been measured. It could match or beat the multimodal model if image features add noise. 3. With one experiment left, only the best accuracy counts. The other untested neighbours have predictable outcomes below 0.725, while this one is genuinely uncertain. It is therefore the option with the most realistic chance of exceeding the current best, while keeping the proven strongest RNA encoder and aggregation.

1) There is no history yet. Every design choice is uncertain: modality, single vs. multi profile, RNA encoder, image encoder, aggregation and fusion. 2) This run tests a strong-prior anchor that combines the choices most likely to help: both modalities, multiple profiles per sample, a scVI RNA embedding, an ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation and simple concat fusion. 3) Only the best accuracy counts, so starting from a likely high performer sets a solid baseline early. Later runs can then remove one choice at a time (unimodal, avgpool, singleprofile, weighted fusion, other encoders) to locate the gains efficiently.

1. Evidence: Only one experiment is done. config_041 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI RNA, ViT-L image, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) reached 0.721 accuracy and 0.681 F1. This is a reasonable baseline, but with a single point we cannot yet tell which design choices matter. 2. What this tests: config_024 keeps every setting identical and swaps only the RNA encoder from scVI to scGPT, a pretrained foundation-model encoder. The one-factor change shows directly whether the RNA representation, plausibly one of the most influential choices, moves performance. 3. Why now: Isolating a high-impact factor early reduces uncertainty efficiently. It may also produce a direct improvement. Whichever encoder wins can then anchor the later tests of fusion, aggregation, image encoder and PCA.

1. Evidence: The two runs share every setting (multiprofile, ViT-L, transformer, concat) except the RNA encoder. scVI-200 reached 0.721 accuracy and scGPT reached 0.507, with F1 agreeing (0.681 vs 0.455). So the RNA encoder looks like a high-impact choice, but the third option, PCA-2000, is still untested. 2. Test: config_007 swaps in PCA-2000 and keeps everything else the same. This completes a clean three-way RNA encoder comparison and shows whether scVI is truly the best RNA representation or whether simple PCA features match or beat it. 3. Why now: The RNA encoder caused a ~21-point swing, so settling this choice early carries the most information. It tells us which RNA encoder to carry into later tests of fusion (weighted), aggregation (avgpool) and image encoder (ResNet50). With 7 experiments left, there is enough budget to exploit the winner afterwards.

Evidence: with the image encoder (ViT-L), aggregation (transformer) and fusion (concat) held fixed, the RNA encoder had a large effect. scVI reached 0.721 accuracy, clearly ahead of PCA at 0.599 and scGPT at 0.507, and F1 followed the same order. scVI is therefore the current best RNA encoder, while fusion, aggregation and image encoder are still untested. This experiment keeps the best configuration (config_041) and changes only fusion, from concat to weighted. That isolates whether the fusion method affects accuracy around the best setup found so far. It is the best use of the next run because it builds directly on a clear lead while answering a key open design question. It also leaves 5 runs to test aggregation (avgpool), the image encoder (ResNet50) or single-profile settings around whichever fusion method wins.

1. Evidence: the RNA encoder clearly matters. scvi_n200 scored about 0.72, against 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt. Fusion matters little: weighted fusion (0.725) and concat (0.721) are within noise. Every run so far has used imagenet_vit_l with transformer aggregation, so the image encoder has not been tested at all. 2. Test: this experiment keeps the best setup (scvi_n200, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion) and swaps the image encoder to resnet50. That isolates whether the ViT-L image features are actually best, or whether resnet50 gives better or comparable features. 3. Why now: the image encoder is the largest untested design choice in the leading setup. Settling it early lets the remaining 5 experiments refine aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) and profile setting around the stronger image backbone, and it avoids spending budget on minor fusion variations.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (about 0.72 vs 0.60 for PCA and 0.51 for scGPT). Fusion (weighted 0.725 vs concat 0.721) and image encoder (ViT-L 0.725 vs ResNet50 0.713) make only small differences. Aggregation has not been varied at all, because every run so far used the transformer. 2) This run keeps the best setup (scvi_n200, ViT-L, weighted fusion, multiprofile) and changes only aggregation to avgpool. That isolates whether the transformer aggregator is actually helping or whether simpler pooling does as well or better. 3) Aggregation is the largest untested design choice inside the best-performing family. 1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (about 0.71–0.725 versus about 0.60 for pca and 0.51 for scgpt). Transformer aggregation beats avgpool, ViT-L slightly beats ResNet50 on accuracy, and weighted fusion is marginally ahead of concat. These last differences are small, so the remaining component choices are nearly settled. The largest open question is the profile setting, since every run so far used multiprofile. 2) This experiment tests singleprofile using the otherwise best components (scvi_n200, ViT-L, weighted fusion), isolating whether multiprofile aggregation actually helps. 3) It is the best use of a limited budget because further fusion or encoder tweaks would likely yield gains of about 0.01 at most. Settling the profile dimension guards against missing a better regime. If singleprofile underperforms, the last 3 runs can refine the multiprofile scvi neighborhood (for example config_006 or rna_only config_039).

Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (about 0.71-0.72 vs 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scgpt). Multiprofile with transformer aggregation is also clearly better than singleprofile (0.54). Fusion type (weighted 0.725 vs concat 0.721) and image encoder (ViT-L 0.725 vs ResNet50 0.713, though ResNet50 had higher F1) made only small differences. That pattern suggests most of the signal may come from the scVI RNA representation, and we have no unimodal baseline. Test: config_039 (RNA-only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, transformer) checks whether the image branch actually adds value or mostly adds noise. Why now: the remaining multimodal scVI variants differ only in components that have shown small effects, so they are unlikely to raise the best result much. This run settles the modality question and has a real chance of matching or beating 0.725 if images contribute little. Either outcome directs the final experiment: refine the multimodal setup if images help, or exploit RNA-only variants if they do not.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 is clearly the strongest RNA encoder (0.70-0.72, versus 0.60 for pca_n2000 and 0.51 for scGPT). Multiprofile transformer aggregation beats avgpool (0.725 vs 0.706) and single-profile (0.537). Fusion type and image encoder each make only small differences. The best result is config_050 (vit_l, weighted, 0.725). config_037 (resnet50, weighted) is close at 0.713 and has the highest F1 (0.695). 2) This experiment: config_006 (scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the only untested setup in the top-performing scvi + multiprofile transformer region. It completes the image-encoder by fusion grid and shows whether resnet50 pairs better with concat, which could give a new best. 3) Why now: with two experiments left, exploiting the strongest region beats exploring weak areas. Those areas include pca_n2000, scGPT, avgpool and image-only models, whose evidence suggests they are unlikely to exceed 0.725.

1) Evidence: scvi_n200 RNA with multiprofile input is clearly the strongest setting. All four scvi multiprofile transformer combinations are already tested (best 0.725, ViT-L with weighted fusion). Weighted fusion has matched or beaten concat in both comparisons (0.725 vs 0.721 with ViT-L, 0.713 vs 0.688 with ResNet50). ResNet50 with weighted fusion gave the highest F1 so far (0.695). Transformer aggregation beat avgpool for ViT-L weighted (0.725 vs 0.706), but only one such comparison exists, and the ResNet50 pairing is untested. 2) Test: config_044 keeps the best-supported choices (scvi_n200, multiprofile, weighted fusion) with ResNet50 features and checks whether avgpool aggregation works better with ResNet50 than it did with ViT-L. 3) Rationale: this is the last experiment, so it should maximise the chance of beating 0.725. pca_n2000 and scgpt encoders have performed far worse, and single-profile and unimodal settings are clearly inferior. The remaining near-top candidates are the scvi multiprofile avgpool variants, and of these, weighted fusion with ResNet50 has the strongest supporting evidence.

My prior is that multimodal, multiprofile models with strong pretrained encoders and learned aggregation tend to do best on cellular profiling tasks. 2) I chose config_005 (multimodal, multiprofile, scVI-200 RNA encoder, ImageNet ViT-L image encoder, transformer aggregation, concat fusion) to set a strong reference point near the likely top of the space. That makes the remaining 9 experiments more informative as targeted one-factor ablations.

1. Evidence: The RNA encoder dominates performance. With the image side fixed at ViT-L, transformer and concat, scVI reached 0.721, against 0.507 for scGPT and 0.599 for PCA. Swapping the image encoder (ViT-L 0.725 vs ResNet50 0.713) and the fusion method (weighted 0.725 vs concat 0.721) changed accuracy by only about 1 point. Transformer aggregation beat avgpool by about 2 points. All six runs so far were multimodal, so we do not know whether the image branch helps or adds noise. 2. Test: Running the best RNA setup alone (scVI, multiprofile, transformer) shows how much the image modality actually contributes. 3.
